title: The Sleeper and the Waker

full_text:
Abu al-Hasan was a merry bachelor of Baghdad who inherited a modest fortune, dividing his life with eccentric order: he lived frugally by day, and every evening invited one stranger to dine with him in his garden pavilion, under the rule that they should never meet again.

One evening, his guest was none other than Caliph Harun al-Rashid in merchant disguise!

Over dinner, Abu al-Hasan confessed his whimsical dream: 'If I were Caliph for just one single day, I would dismiss the corrupt magistrate of our quarter, reward the honest baker, and distribute a thousand dinars to the poor!'

The Caliph slipped a harmless sleeping draught into Abu al-Hasan’s cup. When the host fell into a deep slumber, the Caliph had him carried to the imperial palace, dressed in the royal robes, and laid upon the imperial bed.

At dawn, Abu al-Hasan awoke to the sound of silver flutes! Ministers bowed to the carpet, the Grand Vizier Ja'afar knelt for orders, and courtiers addressed him as Commander of the Faithful!

After pinching his ears and marveling at the miracle, Abu al-Hasan acted with admirable wisdom: he held council, dismissed the corrupt magistrate, rewarded the poor baker, and ordered a thousand dinars sent to Abu al-Hasan’s mother!

That evening, another sleeping potion was administered, and he awoke in his own modest bed in patched sheets.

The resulting confusion of identity delighted all Baghdad. Harun al-Rashid revealed the jest, made Abu al-Hasan his permanent companion at court, and gave him an annual pension, proving that a man who uses power for justice—even in a dream—is worthy of real honor.
moral: Royal power is a heavy mantle of responsibility; true happiness is found in good deeds and contentment.
